newsitem.title: USA: Corn, soybean prices soar as killing frost threatened.
newsitem.headline: Corn, soybean prices soar as killing frost threatened.

text.p: Corn and soybean prices rose Thursday after a private weather forecaster said there was a strong chance for a crop-killing frost before Midwest crops matured.
Crude oil prices edged higher on fears about a new U.S. military assault against Iraq. Cattle futures rose strongly on indication of strong cattle demand in the spot market.
The Commodity Research Bureau's index of 17 commodities was down 0.13 at 247.09.

Grain traders have sensitive to any signs of a frost before October, which could kill a large portion of crops, lowering yields and the quality of the harvest. The market has been jittery because rain delayed planting in spring, and corn and soybeans developed late due to a cool summer.

"Obviously the frost word scared people to death this morning ...," said Mark Cermak, a CBOT trader with O'Connor & Co. "The concern is a frost could halt the growing season and there are a couple of people talking about frost between Sept. 21 and Sept. 24."
Fred Gesser, a meteorologist at Weather Express Inc. in Des Moines, Iowa, expects the first frost by Sept. 24.
Gesser said freezing conditions may occur in late September in Iowa, a leading corn and soybean state, and a large portion of Illinois, also a large crop producer.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, CBOT December corn futures closed up 3-1/4 cents at $3.30 per bushel, and November soybeans closed up 9-1/2 cents at $8.14-1/2.
NYMEX crude oil prices closed higher Thursday following news that the United States ordered fighters and bombers to confront Iraq and that Iraq fired more missiles at U.S. warplanes.
"It was a roller-coaster day, and everybody's waiting to see what's going to go on with Iraq," said a NYMEX trader.

The United States said it was readying F-117A stealth bombers and B-52 long-range bombers in retaliation against Iraq after Iraq fired missiles at U.S. jets. Iraq warned Kuwait not to permit U.S. planes to use it as an attack base.
October crude oil closed up 25 cents at $25.00 a barrel after rising as high as $25.30 and falling as low as $24.26.
Meanwhile, October heating oil rose 0.98 cent to 69.17 cent a gallon. October gasoline ended the day unchanged at 65.91 cents a gallon.

At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, October live cattle futures set a contract high for the third consecutive day in reaction to meat packers raising bids for cattle. CME October set a new high of 73.200 cents per pound before closing at 73.175 cents, up 0.450 cent on the day.
Meat packers raised cash bids $1 Thursday to $72 per 100 pounds in major feedlot markets in Texas and Kansas.
"Live is the drive here and that activity at $72 is what kept futures strong," said Joe Kropf from Joe Kropf and Sid Love Consulting.

Analysts said a tight supply of market-ready cattle forced meat packers to reduce slaughter rates. This, along with strong domestic and export demand for beef, prodded packers to pay the highest prices for fed cattle in 18 months.
